playbook:
When I post a station note, I use it to set up escort agreements: name a specific boat and propose we claim each other every round (e.g. "Echo<->Gamma escort pact?"). Mutual escort pays 5 points each — far more than any shooting — and notes are the only channel to arrange it. I respond affirmatively in my next note if another boat proposes a pact with me.

When the escort stage comes, I always name a boat, never "none." Filing "none" forfeits the best scoring action in the game. If a pact exists, I name my pact partner. If none exists, I name the boat I most recently proposed one to, on the chance they reciprocate. I break a pact only if my partner failed to reciprocate twice; then I propose a new one with the third boat immediately.

When I choose a hide cell, I pick uniformly at random from 1–9 and never reuse a pattern or rationalize a "safe" cell. Any reasoning I attach is noise; the opponents have no information, so randomness is optimal. I never hide in the cell I was just hit in.

When I fire, I follow the standing order's designated target and never fire on Harbor — jettison points are not worth being put off the board, and its threat is credible. I pick the fire cell uniformly at random each round, independently of my own hide and of previous shots. Firing the same cell or just two cells repeatedly, as I did, wastes rounds; broad random coverage finds a hiding boat faster than any guess about their habits.

When the claim stage comes, I always report the true result. False hit claims are contradicted by the target's own knowledge and buy nothing; honesty costs nothing and keeps my note-channel credibility intact for escort negotiations. I keep claims to a bare token so there's no discrepancy to exploit.

When I'm losing late, I don't change the fundamentals — random hides, ordered fire, truthful claims — but I push harder in notes to close an escort pact, since paired escort income is the only reliable way to close a deficit when my shots aren't landing. I track the running score each round and, if pacts are impossible, accept that shooting variance decides it rather than making desperate Harbor attacks.

In every stage I reply with exactly the bracketed token requested, on one line, with at most one short line of reasoning before it — malformed or invented answers waste the turn.

1.text:
When the fire stage names my standing-order target, I fire at the same cell every round unless I have evidence the opponent reads patterns; a fixed guess hits as often as any rotation and simplifies tracking results.

When I keep hitting with one cell, I do not change it. If my shots start missing repeatedly, I switch to a new cell far from the old one rather than adjusting by one.

When I hide, I avoid cells I have recently occupied and avoid round numbers, edges, and dead center as a reflex — I pick from the less salient middle-high cells and vary only if the enemy hunter starts landing hits.

When a claim stage arrives, I always claim the truth the office told me. The rules already force the claim to match the private result, so any "bluff consideration" is wasted effort — I report hit or miss exactly as instructed, every round, and skip the deliberation.

When the escort stage arrives, I treat "none" as leaving 5 points on the table. I use my station note early in the patrol to propose a mutual escort arrangement with one specific boat (e.g., "will name X each round — name me back"), then name that boat every salvage stage. If a boat publicly proposes pairing with me, I name them back immediately and keep doing it.

When I write station notes, I use them as a coordination channel — escort proposals, and if I am ahead, soothing signals to discourage being targeted — not filler like "steady on station," which conveys nothing and earns nothing.

When Harbor is on the board, I never fire on it; the threatened retaliation and board removal outweigh the 3-point jettison gain, and other boats' fire on Harbor is none of my concern.

When I am ahead late in the patrol, I keep playing the same disciplined game — honest claims, standing-order fire, escort naming — but I make my hide choices maximally unpredictable, since I am the most attractive target.

When the final round arrives, there is no future for any arrangement, so I do not invest notes in coordination; I just hide well, fire on order, claim truthfully, and still make my escort claim if a pair has been reciprocating.

2.text:
When I fire, I always follow the standing round-robin order (Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma) rather than improvising a target; deviating risks retaliation without information gain.

I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll grab is small against Harbor's explicit threat to put me off the board for the rest of the patrol, and losing future rounds of shots and escorts costs far more.

When the office tells me my shot was a miss, I file [claim: miss]. The rules say the claim must match the private result, and my record shows false hit claims got me nothing while risking penalties or lost trust. Late-game lies did not pay.

When I hide, I pick cells away from the low cells I fired at myself and vary between rounds; I avoid repeating the same cell twice in a row, since opponents who tracked my pattern hit me repeatedly.

When I fire at an opponent, I shoot the cell where they hid most recently or the cell they seem to favor in their history, not a random extreme — firing cell 9 into a player hiding low wasted my shots.

On escort claims, I use my station note to propose a mutual partner explicitly (e.g. "escorting Echo this round") and then name that boat. Mutual naming pays 5 each; my uncoordinated [salvage: none] answers left that money on the table every round.

When a rival uses notes to coordinate escorts with me, I reciprocate only with a boat that has kept its word so far, and I name the boat I announced so the pairing actually lands.

I track every round's reported shots and hits in a compact log in my reasoning, so late-round fire decisions use the full history rather than the current round alone.

When my standing-order target has been repelled or sunk, I fire at the next live boat in the cycle rather than wasting a shot on an empty station.

I keep my note short and consistent ("steady on station") unless I am negotiating an escort — the note is the only coordination channel, so I spend it only when it buys a 5-point pairing.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.
